abstract: Background: prolonged intermittent theta burst stimulation (piTBS), as used in Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT), achieves antidepressant efficacy, yet its acute single-session mechanisms remain elusive. EEG can capture online oscillatory dynamics during piTBS and pre- to post-stimulation changes in TMS-evoked cortical reactivity. Methods: in a randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial, 40 healthy males completed two visits ( [≥]7-day washout), receiving active or sham piTBS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Inter-train EEG power was analyzed across three blocks of 20 trains in 37 participants. Pre- and post-stimulation measures of TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), working memory and sustained attention were analyzed in all 40 participants. Results: left frontal theta power followed different trajectories across blocks during active and sham piTBS (conditionxblock interaction, p = .014). During active piTBS, theta power was below baseline in blocks 1 and 2 and increased significantly from block 2 to block 3. Across conditions, alpha power was lower in blocks 2 and 3 than in block 1. Direct comparison of pre-to-post TEP changes between active and sham piTBS identified no significant clusters in the N45, P60, N100 and P180 component windows. Exploratory analyses within active piTBS identified a decrease in frontal N100 cluster amplitude and an increase in posterior N100 cluster amplitude. Neither behavioral outcome showed condition-dependent changes. Conclusion: a single session of active piTBS modulated left frontal theta power between stimulation trains. Whether this early response is associated with cumulative plasticity or antidepressant outcomes following SNT warrants further investigation.
